flashcards.q: Random forest ensemble variance formula and what it implies about feature subsampling?
flashcards.a: rho*sigma^2 + (1-rho)*sigma^2/k -- as k->infinity the floor is rho*sigma^2, not zero. Row bootstrapping alone leaves trees correlated (rho high); random feature subsets per split are needed to actually decorrelate and let averaging shrink variance.

flashcards.q: Why do bootstrap samples leave out ~36.8% of rows (OOB), exactly?
flashcards.a: P(a row never selected in n draws with replacement from n rows) = (1-1/n)^n -> 1/e ~ 0.368 as n grows. These out-of-bag rows give a free validation estimate per tree.

flashcards.q: Gradient boosting: what does each new tree fit, and what does it reduce (bias or variance)?
flashcards.a: Each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss w.r.t. the current ensemble's predictions (= ordinary residual for squared error). Reduces BIAS sequentially; needs regularization (eta, depth, subsampling) or variance blows up.

flashcards.q: XGBoost histogram binning: what's the complexity win and the accuracy cost?
flashcards.a: Bins continuous features into max_bin=256 buckets by default, cutting split search from O(n log n) to O(bins) per feature. Cost: split can only land on a bucket boundary, a bounded approximation of at most one bucket's width vs the exact optimal threshold.

flashcards.q: XGBoost leaf weight closed form and its connection to ridge regression?
flashcards.a: w* = -sum(g_i)/(sum(h_i)+lambda), from the 2nd-order Taylor approx of the loss. Same mechanism as ridge's (X^T X + lambda*I): adding lambda to a denominator/matrix shrinks the estimate toward zero and stabilizes thinly-supported leaves.

flashcards.q: LightGBM leaf-wise vs level-wise growth -- why does num_leaves matter more than max_depth?
flashcards.a: Leaf-wise always expands the single globally-best leaf, producing deep asymmetric trees for a fixed leaf count -- max_depth doesn't bound total leaves the way it does for level-wise growth. num_leaves (default 31) is the real capacity control; rule of thumb num_leaves < 2^max_depth.

flashcards.q: GOSS mechanism and why it reweights instead of dropping low-gradient rows?
flashcards.a: Keeps all top-a% high-gradient rows, samples fraction b of the rest, reweights sampled low-gradient rows by (1-a)/b to keep the expected gradient sum for split-finding unbiased -- dropping without reweighting would systematically underestimate their contribution.

flashcards.q: EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling) -- what does it target and why?
flashcards.a: Bundles mutually-exclusive sparse features (canonically one-hot encoded categoricals, at most one nonzero per row) into a single feature via value-range offsetting, reducing effective column count for histogram building on high-cardinality categorical data.

flashcards.q: What is CatBoost's 'prediction shift' and how does ordered boosting fix it?
flashcards.a: Standard boosting's residual for row i uses a model that already partially learned from row i's own label in earlier trees, producing systematic optimism. Ordered boosting computes row i's gradient using only a model trained on rows preceding i in a random permutation -- no row's label ever contributes to its own gradient.

flashcards.q: CatBoost symmetric (oblivious) trees -- what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Same feature+threshold at every node of a given depth -> fast vectorized leaf lookup at inference and implicit regularization, but cannot express splits that vary by region the way an unconstrained tree can -- a representational cost for a speed/regularization gain.

flashcards.q: Default library pick heuristic: large mostly-numeric data, high-cardinality categoricals, safest all-around?
flashcards.a: LightGBM first for large/mostly-numeric (speed); CatBoost first for high-cardinality categorical-heavy data (native handling, ordered target statistics); XGBoost as the safest all-around default with the most mature tooling.
